transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, doctor, my family insisted I come down here, though if you ask me, it's a whole lot of fuss over absolutely nothing. They keep telling me—my wife, my kids—they keep saying I’m doing too much. Doing too much, can you believe that? At seventy-four, you’d think they’d be thrilled I’m not just sitting in a recliner wasting away watching television all day. But to me, honestly, it just feels like I’m the only one left in the world with enough drive to actually get anything accomplished. 

Take this move we're doing, for example. It’s a massive undertaking, sorting through decades of things, and nobody else was stepping up to coordinate the logistics, so I had to take the reins to get the whole move handled. And then there's the new place—the garage wasn't built right, the framing was completely sloppy, so I’ve been out there pulling it apart and rebuilding the new garage right, all by myself. You can't trust these modern contractors, you know? You have to do it yourself if you want a structure to last. 

And on top of that, I’ve had to step in and organize things over at the church because the committee was just dragging their feet on the community outreach program, sitting around talking in circles. And I'm still working, you know, down at the plant running the mixing and grinding equipment. I have to be there to show the younger fellows at work how the job actually ought to be done, because they just don't have the work ethic anymore. They stand around looking at their phones while I'm doing the work of three men! So, sure, I'm busy. I've got a lot on my plate. But someone has to do it, and they want to send me to a doctor just for having a little gumption!
Have you had any arguments with your family about your activities lately?

Arguments? Well, I suppose they would call them arguments, yes. But from where I’m standing, it’s just that I’ve been feeling like everybody needs to either get on board with my plans or just get the heck out of my way. 

I mean, I’ll be having a great day, right? Just feeling fantastic. Honestly, I’ll be out there working, joking around with the guys at the plant or whistling out in the yard, just feeling ten feet tall. I feel like I have more energy and clear-headedness than I did when I was thirty! I feel completely unstoppable, getting things done left and right, running the show exactly how it ought to be run. 

But then, sure enough, here comes my wife, or my boy, David, walking out to the driveway to interrupt me. David came over just the other day—it must have been Tuesday, because he always takes that route home on Tuesdays after his meetings—and he starts asking me these completely pointless little questions about whether I’m pacing myself, or how I’m sorting the moving boxes, or if I measured the headers right for the new garage. And I just... I go from joking and feeling on top of the world to just snapping at my wife or my boy over some little question. I really bit David's head off, and then I snapped at my wife when she came out to tell me dinner was getting cold. 

I just don't have the patience for it right now! If you’re feeling ten feet tall and you’re actually making real progress on a half-dozen important things, the last thing you want is someone picking at you with little questions like you don't know what you're doing. So, yes, we’ve had some words, and I've been losing my temper a bit, but if they would just pitch in or step aside, there wouldn't be any friction at all!
When did you start feeling like you had more energy and could get so much done?

Well, let me think back on the timeline here... it’s been about a month now. Yes, I'd say exactly a month, because it all really kicked into high gear right when we were forced to start leaving the old house. 

And let me tell you, doctor, that whole situation with the house was an absolute debacle. We didn't want to leave, you know. We had been in that home for decades. You build a life in a place, you get the landscaping just right, you insulate the windows yourself so they don't draft in the winter... but once the decision came down and our hands were tied, and we were forced to start packing up our entire lives, well, it was a mess. I looked around at my wife, who was just completely overwhelmed, practically paralyzed by the sheer volume of things to sort through, and I realized someone had to take the bull by the horns. 

It was about four weeks ago, a Tuesday or a Wednesday, I believe, and I just woke up and the energy was there. It was like a switch flipped in my brain. I realized I couldn't just sit around and wait for the movers or for my kids to figure it out at their own sluggish pace. So I started cataloging the basement, and then I moved to the attic, and honestly, since that day a month ago, I haven't needed to slow down for a single second. The energy just keeps building! 

Because there is just so much to do, you see? You have to coordinate the trucks, you have to sort the hardware—I had coffee cans full of heavy-duty screws and brass fittings down in my workshop that you just can't even buy anymore, and you think I'm going to let some minimum-wage mover toss those in a cardboard box willy-nilly? Absolutely not. I had to inventory all of it. So, yes, a month. A month of solid, productive, unstoppable work ever since we had to start moving out of that house, and frankly, I haven't felt this sharp or capable in my entire life.
Have you been sleeping less than usual over the past month?

Sleep? Well, now that you mention it... I suppose I haven't really been paying much attention to the clock at night. You see, when you have this much going on, when you're managing a move of this magnitude, rebuilding a garage from the studs up, keeping the plant running, and trying to get a church committee to actually do something besides eat donuts and argue about the budget... sleep just doesn't seem like the priority it used to be. 

I mean, I'll lay down in bed, sure. My wife, she insists on it. She says, "Arthur, it's midnight, you need to rest." So I'll lay there, staring at the ceiling, but my mind is just racing, calculating the load-bearing capacity of those headers I put up, or figuring out the best route for the moving truck to avoid that construction on Route 9. And after maybe an hour, two at the most, I just think, what is the point of laying here in the dark when there are three perfectly good hours before dawn where I could be getting things done? 

So I get up. I go out to the workshop, or I start packing up the good china—which, by the way, you cannot trust anyone else to pack. My daughter-in-law offered, but she just tosses things in with a single sheet of newspaper! It’s criminal. So I do it myself, at three in the morning, humming along to the radio. And the funny thing is, doctor, I don't feel tired! Not even a little bit. I used to need a solid seven hours, maybe even a nap in the recliner after Sunday dinner, but now? Now I'm running on a couple hours here and there, and I feel like a steam engine going full tilt! So, yes, I suppose I am sleeping less, but frankly, I don't miss it one bit. Who needs sleep when you have this much momentum?
Have you experienced any periods of feeling sad or depressed over the past year?

Sad? Depressed? Well, no, not really. I mean, sure, everyone gets a little down in the dumps sometimes, right? Like when the weather is bad for a week straight and you can't get out to work on the yard, or when the guys at the plant are being particularly pig-headed about a new procedure. But depressed? No, I wouldn't say that. 

I mean, look at me! I'm 74 years old, I'm still working the grinding machines at the plant—and let me tell you, those machines require a delicate touch, a real understanding of the material, whether you're polishing steel or blending compounds. You can't just slap any young kid in front of a grinder and expect a smooth finish. It takes years of experience, decades even, to get the feel for it. And I've still got it! I've got more energy and focus than guys half my age. 

So, no, I haven't been sitting around moping or feeling sorry for myself. I don't have time for that! There's just too much to do, too much to accomplish. Even with this whole moving debacle, which, as I said, was a real headache, I didn't get depressed about it. I got angry, sure, and frustrated with the sheer incompetence of everyone around me, but I didn't get sad. I just rolled up my sleeves and got to work. 

You see, doctor, I've always believed that idle hands are the devil's workshop. If you're feeling a little low, the worst thing you can do is sit around and stew in it. You have to get up, get moving, tackle a project. That's what I did when we had to leave the house, and that's what I do every day. I keep my mind sharp, my hands busy, and I just keep pushing forward. So, no, no depression here. Just a whole lot of momentum!
Do you feel like you're sleeping less because you're busy or because you don't feel like you need as much sleep as you used to?

Well, that's an interesting way to put it, doctor. It's a bit of both, isn't it? But if I really sit down and think about it—not that I do a lot of sitting these days—it's definitely because I just don't need the sleep. 

I mean, yes, I am incredibly busy. Like I said, I've got the move, the garage, the plant, the church committee... and just last week, I started organizing my entire collection of vintage Popular Mechanics magazines. I've got issues going back to 1968, and they were just sitting in boxes! You can't just leave history like that in a cardboard box where the silverfish can get to it. So I've been building custom shelving for them, measuring out the exact dimensions so they fit perfectly, and let me tell you, getting the right kind of lumber for a project like that these days is a nightmare. You go to the hardware store and it's all warped pine! You have to really dig to find a straight board. 

But even with all of that going on, even with my plate completely full, the real reason I'm up at three in the morning is that my body just doesn't want to sleep. It's not like I'm forcing myself to stay awake because I have a deadline. It's not like when I was younger and I'd have to pull a double shift at the plant and I'd be drinking terrible break-room coffee just to keep my eyes open. No, no, no. This is entirely different. 

I lay down, and I feel like I've just had a full eight hours of rest, even if I've only been asleep for forty-five minutes. My eyes pop open, my brain is firing on all cylinders, and I just feel this... this surge of readiness. It's like my battery is fully charged in record time. Why would I stay in bed when I feel so fantastic? When I have so much energy? So, yes, I'm busy, busier than I've been in years, but I'm sleeping less because I genuinely, honestly, just do not need it anymore. It's the most remarkable thing, really.
Do you feel like you're more important or capable than others around you, now more than ever before?

Important? No, no, I wouldn't use a word like that. I'm not the President, I'm just Arthur. I'm a guy who works the grinding machines. I don't think I'm some hotshot or... or better than anybody else, if that's what you're getting at. 

Now, capable? Well, sure I'm capable! But doctor, I've always been capable. That isn't anything new. You don't survive in the manufacturing business, working with heavy machinery, blending industrial compounds for decades, if you aren't capable. I mean, I remember back in, oh, it must have been '88 or '89, they brought in this new line of automated polishers at the plant, and the manuals were all translated poorly from German. Half the guys on the floor were ready to walk out because the machines kept jamming and ruining the stock. Who do you think figured out the feed rate issue? I did. I sat there for two days with a caliper and a notebook and I figured it out. I've always been the guy people come to when they need something done right. 

So do I feel more capable now than I ever did before? Not really, no. My skills haven't magically changed overnight. I don't suddenly have a degree in structural engineering just because I'm rebuilding my garage from the studs up. I'm just using the knowledge I've accumulated over seventy-four years on this earth. The only difference is, like I said, I've got the momentum to actually get to all these projects now! I'm not sitting around watching television like most guys my age. I'm putting my skills to work. 

I mean, look at the church committee. Am I more important than Pastor Miller? Of course not, it's his church. But when they sit around for three hours debating whether to use paper plates or styrofoam for the Sunday pancake breakfast, someone has to step up and make a practical decision! It’s just common sense. I don't think I'm a superhero or anything, I just have a very low tolerance for people dragging their feet when there's work to be done. So, no, I'm not more important, and my capabilities are the exact same as they've always been. I just happen to be firing on all cylinders while everyone else is still trying to find the ignition!
Do you feel like you can accomplish anything you set your mind to, without any limitations?

Without any limitations? Well, now, let's not get carried away, doctor. I'm a practical man, not a... a magician. I mean, I can't just step out the window and fly, and I'm certainly not going to go build a rocket ship in my backyard. You have to respect the materials you're working with, whether that's in life or in the shop. 

Take the grinding wheels down at the plant, for instance. You've got your aluminum oxide wheels, your silicon carbide... you have to know their absolute limits. You push a wheel past its maximum RPM rating because you think you can just "accomplish anything," and you know what happens? It shatters. Shrapnel everywhere. I saw a guy, Jimmy—oh, this was back in the late seventies—he thought he could rush a heavy slag removal job. He didn't respect the limitations of the machine or the laws of physics. Nearly lost an eye. So, no, I don't think I can do just *anything*. 

And even with my projects at home, like the custom shelving for those vintage magazines I was telling you about, I still have to measure twice and cut once. The wood grain dictates what you can and can't do. You can't force a piece of warped pine to be perfectly straight just by setting your mind to it! It's going to bow, it's going to crack, it's going to fight you the whole way. You have to work *with* the physical reality of the thing. You learn that in your first week on any job site. 

So, sure, I feel incredibly sharp right now, and I'm getting through my to-do list faster than I have in twenty years, but I know my boundaries. The laws of the universe still apply to Arthur, I assure you. I just happen to know how to operate right up to the very edge of those limits without crossing over into foolishness. That's what experience gives you. So, no, I don't think I'm limitless. I just know exactly what I'm doing, and I'm not wasting a single second getting it done.
Have you noticed any changes in your appetite over the past month?

Appetite? Well, no, not that I can think of. I mean, a machine needs fuel, right? Just like the heavy-duty blenders and grinders down at the shop. You don't feed them the right power, they don't run. I've always been a meat and potatoes kind of guy, and that certainly hasn't changed one bit. 

I still have my two eggs and a piece of rye toast every single morning. Now, I might be eating it standing up at the kitchen counter these days instead of sitting at the table, just because I'm busy mapping out the schematics for those magazine shelves I mentioned, but I eat it all the same. And lunch... well, I still have my soup—usually chicken noodle, sometimes beef barley if they have it on sale at the grocery store—just like I've done for forty-something years at the plant. You get into a rhythm, you know? The body expects fuel at noon, and I give it fuel at noon. 

Even with all the projects I'm getting done, I haven't lost my taste for a good meal. I don't skip meals, doctor. That's how you get sloppy, and sloppy leads to mistakes when you're working with power tools or heavy equipment. I saw a fella once—this was back in the early nineties, I think—he decided to work right through his lunch break to finish up a batch of industrial solvent we were mixing. He got the shakes from not eating, dropped a fifty-pound bag of caustic powder, and we had to evacuate the whole floor. Total disaster, and all because he didn't stop for a sandwich. 

So, no, I respect the machinery of my own body. I eat my three square meals just like I always have. I might be burning through it a little faster with all the sawing and hammering I'm doing, but my actual appetite? Nothing different about it at all.
Have you made any large or impulsive purchases over the past month?

Impulsive? Well, I don't know if I'd use a word like impulsive. An impulse is buying a pack of gum at the checkout counter. What I'm doing is... well, it's logistics. It's project management. Now, did I put some deposits down recently? Yes. Yes, I did. I put down a fair bit of money to get the garage work moving—getting the foundation poured right and the framing started—and I bought some heavy-duty equipment for it. We're talking a high-capacity air compressor, a commercial-grade drill press, professional stuff. You can't do a job right with cheap, hardware-store tools, doctor, you just can't. 

Now, did I talk it over with my wife first? Well... no. No, I didn't. But you have to understand, if I stop to explain the torque specifications of a new drill press to her, the contractor is going to book someone else, and the equipment goes off sale! You have to strike while the iron is hot. So I just handled it. I wrote the checks. She wasn't exactly thrilled when she saw the bank statements, but she'll see the value when it's all finished and we have a proper workspace. 

And because I've got all this going on, I've been... well, I've been moving fast. There aren't enough hours in the day, so I kept driving back and forth between the houses—our main place and the property where the garage is being rebuilt—just trying to coordinate the deliveries and keep the contractors on schedule. It's a thirty-minute drive, but if you hit the lights right and don't get stuck behind some Sunday driver, you can make it in twenty. 

And, well, I suppose I was bringing that same energy down to the plant, too. I had to get my shifts done so I could get back out to the builds, so I was rushing some of the grinding jobs at work. Just pushing the feed rates a little higher than standard protocol, getting the batches blended and out the door faster. Some of the guys on the floor, and the shift foreman, they actually pulled me aside. They warned me I was taking chances. 'Arthur, you're going to burn out the motor,' they said. 'Arthur, you're taking risks, you're going too fast.' But they don't see the big picture! They don't understand that when you have this kind of momentum, you have to use it. You can't just sit on your hands and do things at a snail's pace when there's real work to be done. So, yes, I spent some money on the deposits, and I've been rushing around a bit, but it's all for a purpose. You can't build anything lasting without making a few waves.
Have you ever heard voices or seen things that weren't there?

Voices? Like... people talking when nobody's around? No, no, nothing like that. Now, I will say, my hearing isn't exactly what it used to be—you spend half a century around industrial crushing equipment and heavy-duty mixers, and you see how your ears fare. We didn't always have the fancy, government-mandated ear protection they force on you on the floor today. Back in the seventies, you just stuffed a bit of cotton in there, or maybe those little cheap foam plugs if the foreman happened to have a box in his office, and you just dealt with the noise. 

So, do I hear a ringing sometimes? Sure I do. It’s a high-pitched whine, almost exactly like the sound of a diamond-tipped blade cutting through hardened steel. Sometimes I'll be sitting in my living room at night, quiet as a mouse, and I'll hear that hum. But that’s just wear and tear on the eardrums, doctor. That’s just physics. It’s certainly not voices. I’ve never had anyone whispering in my ear or... or telling me things from the great beyond. I only listen to the machines, and they only tell you when they need oil or a new belt. 

And as for seeing things that aren't there... well, you have to have incredibly sharp eyes in my line of work, and I still do. You miss a hairline fracture on a polishing wheel, and like I was saying earlier, it's a disaster waiting to happen. So my eyes are always locked in on the physical reality of the materials. Now, sometimes, if I've been staring at the sparks flying off a piece of carbon steel for three or four hours straight, trying to get a batch rushed out the door, I might close my eyes and still see the afterimage. You know what I mean? Like when you look at a bright lightbulb and look away, and you have that spot floating in your vision. Or if you get a speck of aluminum dust in your eye because your safety goggles aren't seated right on the bridge of your nose—I'm always telling the young guys, "seat your goggles, or you'll be seeing spots for a week"—but that's just biology. It’s a physical reaction. It’s not... visions. I don't see ghosts or things floating around the room. 

I'm a practical man, doctor. Mechanics, materials, tangible things. If I can't measure it with a pair of calipers or put a heavy-duty level on it, it simply isn't there. So no, my mind isn't playing any tricks on me. I'm completely grounded in the real world, I'm just moving through it a lot faster than everyone else right now.
Do you feel like your contributions and accomplishments are more significant than those of others around you?

More significant? Well, no. I mean, what does that even mean, really? You see, doctor, when you work in an industrial setting—and I’ve been on the floor for, gosh, over fifty years now—you learn pretty quickly that every single gear in the machine has to turn, or the whole thing just completely grinds to a halt. 

I’m a grinder and a mixer. I take raw materials, I get the exact right consistency, I polish things down to a fraction of a millimeter. Is that important? Absolutely. If I mess up a batch of industrial compound, if the viscosity is off even by a hair, the whole assembly line down the chain has to stop. But... is it more significant than the guy driving the forklift? Or the fella loading the pallets? Not a chance. 

Let me tell you about a guy we had named Mickey. This was back in... oh, it must have been 1982, maybe '83. Mickey was just the floor sweeper. I had a couple semesters of college under my belt before I realized I was better with my hands, but Mickey, I don't even think he finished high school. He just pushed a broom. But one day, Mickey called in sick, and the shift manager didn't bother to replace him for the day. Thought we could just do without. Well, by 2 PM, there was so much fine aluminum dust built up near the ventilation grates from the polishing wheels that one stray spark from a loose drive belt could have taken the roof right off the building. It's highly combustible, you see. The foreman had to shut down production for three whole hours just so we could all grab brooms and clear the floor. So, you tell me, was my job running the heavy-duty mixer more significant than Mickey's job pushing that broom? No. Not at all. It's a system. 

It’s the exact same thing with these projects I’m doing now. Sure, I’m the one drawing up the schematics for the garage, and I’m the one pushing the pace and getting the equipment, but I still need the concrete guys to pour the foundation right. If their mix is off, if it doesn't cure right, my framing doesn't matter one bit. I don't think I'm some... some king of the factory or a master architect. I don't think I'm better than anybody else. I'm just a guy who knows how to work hard and get things done. 

Now, I might be getting a lot *more* done right now than the younger guys on the floor, just because I don't stop and they spend half their shift looking at their cellular phones, but that’s just a matter of basic work ethic. That's not me being some sort of superior being. I just do my job, doctor. Always have. You just put your head down, you check your calibrations, and you do the work. Everybody's got a part to play.
Are you finding that your increased energy and activity level is causing problems for you at work or in your relationships with family and friends?

Problems? Well... I suppose that depends entirely on who you happen to be asking, doctor. If you ask me, I’m just being remarkably efficient. But if you ask the people around me... well, yes, there’s been a fair bit of friction lately. I won't deny that. 

Let's start with the plant. I mentioned earlier that I was pushing the feed rates on the grinders, trying to get those batches out the door so I could get back to the property and manage the contractors. Well, the shift foreman—fella named Dave, been there about fifteen years, good guy but a real stickler for the corporate safety handbook—he didn't just stop at giving me a warning. See, I had the RPMs cranked up on the main polishing wheel, just trying to power through a heavy load of tungsten carbide pieces. You have to understand, tungsten carbide is incredibly dense, it takes absolutely forever if you run it at the standard speed. So I bumped it up. And, well, the motor started smoking. Just a little bit! Nothing a quick cool-down wouldn't fix, but Dave saw the smoke, panicked, hit the emergency stop, and blew the whole breaker for that side of the floor. Next thing I know, I'm sitting in the front office, and they’re telling me I’m being pulled from work entirely. Sent me home pending a full review over a "safety incident." Can you believe that? Over fifty years I've been running those machines, and they pull me off the line for trying to improve efficiency.

And then, of course, I get home, and things aren't any better there. My wife, she had already been stewing over those deposits I made for the garage equipment, like I told you. But then she gets on the telephone, calls up our son and our daughter, and suddenly it's a whole family tribunal. They sit me down at my own kitchen table and tell me things have gotten "out of hand." That was their exact phrase. Out of hand. 

So now, they’ve completely stopped trusting me with any of the decisions. My own family! They took the checkbook and the credit cards, so I can't manage the money for the build anymore—which is ridiculous because the contractors need to be paid on time or they walk. And the driving! I told you I was making that drive between the houses in twenty minutes, right? Well, my daughter decides that means I'm some sort of hazard on the road, so they're trying to keep the keys to the truck from me. They don't want me driving at all. And the move itself, the whole transition to the new property... they've just completely cut me out of the logistics. They say I'm moving too fast, that I'm not thinking things through, that I'm taking too many risks. So, yes, I suppose my energy is causing problems, but only because nobody else seems to have the stamina to keep up with the pace!
Are you feeling like your family and friends are understanding and supportive of your current activities and pace?

Supportive? Doctor, I feel like I'm speaking a completely different language than the rest of them. Like I was just telling you about the checkbook and the keys... that’s not support. That’s a blockade. It’s like... well, it’s like trying to run a heavy-duty mixer when someone keeps sneaking around back and yanking the power cord out of the wall. You just can’t get any momentum going. 

My son, for instance. He is a good boy, I raised him right, but he’s an accountant. Sits in a nice, climate-controlled office all day long looking at spreadsheets and drinking fancy coffee. He doesn't know the first thing about project management in the physical world. He doesn't understand that when you have a window of good weather in the late fall, you have to pour the concrete right then and there. You can't form a committee and think about it for three weeks. If the ground freezes before it cures, your foundation cracks, and then where are you? You're out ten thousand dollars and you have to jackhammer the whole mess up, that's where. But I try to explain this to him, and he just gives me this... this look. Like I'm a total stranger speaking Greek. 

And my wife, bless her, we have been married a long time, but she has always been the cautious type. Always wanting to wait and see. She keeps telling me we should just wait until spring to finish the garage. Wait until spring! Doctor, do you have any earthly idea what happens to the price of treated lumber in the spring? The demand goes completely through the roof because every weekend warrior in a ten-mile radius decides they want to build a deck. You buy your materials now, in the off-season, when the supply yards are desperate to clear out their inventory before the snow flies. It’s just basic economics. It’s common sense. 

But do they see that? Do they appreciate the thousands of dollars I am saving us by pushing the schedule? No. Not at all. They just see me getting up early, making things happen, moving at a pace they simply do not have the stamina to match. And instead of pitching in, instead of grabbing a hammer or helping me load the truck, they decide I'm the problem. They decide I need to be stopped. So no, they don't understand it at all. I am practically dragging this entire family kicking and screaming toward a better, more organized future, and all I get for my trouble is a tribunal at my own kitchen table.
Are you finding that your current activities and pace are affecting your ability to get along with others or perform your job effectively?

Well, like I was just saying with the tribunal and Dave pulling me off the line... obviously, it’s affecting things. But you have to look at the root cause of it, doctor. The way I see it, I’ve just been feeling like everybody needs to either get on board with my plans or get out of my way. It’s really that simple. We have a timeline, we have materials to stage, we have a whole life to organize! 

And I'll admit, my patience isn't what it usually is. It’s strange, because half the time I feel absolutely fantastic. Better than fantastic. I’ll be up at four in the morning, making the coffee, making a list for the day, and I'm joking around, whistling... I feel ten feet tall! I really do. I feel like I could lift a Buick over my head and still have energy to pour a driveway. I haven't felt this sharp or this capable in decades. 

But then... well, then the rest of the world wakes up. My wife will come downstairs, or my boy will call me on the telephone, and they’ll interrupt me with some little question. Just something completely trivial, like, "Did you call the insurance agent back?" or "Are you sure about the dimensions on the roof pitch?" Just some little question that doesn't matter in the grand scheme of everything I'm trying to accomplish. And I just... I snap at them. I'll go straight from joking and feeling ten feet tall to just biting their heads off. 

I did the exact same thing to Dave on the floor right before he hit the emergency stop on my grinder. He came over asking some little question about the feed rate, and I just barked right at him. I can't seem to help it. It’s like... it's like my brain is moving at a hundred miles an hour, and they're all stuck in a school zone, and when they try to pull me down to their speed, I just get so incredibly irritated. If they would just pitch in and move at my pace, or at least just step aside and let me work, we wouldn't have any of these problems. But because they insist on dragging their feet and second-guessing every move I make, yes, there is a lot of snapping going on.
Are you finding it difficult to wind down and relax, even when you're not working on a project?

Wind down? Relax? Doctor, I honestly don't even know what those words mean right now. My wife, she’ll say to me, "Just sit in the recliner for a bit, watch a television program with me, just take a breath." And I try, I really do try to humor her. I'll sit down in the chair. But I swear to you, I can’t seem to sit in that chair for more than maybe two or three minutes before I’m right back up on my feet. 

The second my rear end hits the cushion, my mind is already out in the hallway with the packing. I start thinking about how the boxes aren't categorized properly, so I’m up sorting boxes—making sure the heavy hardware is in the double-corrugated ones so the bottoms don't fall out, because nobody else thinks of that.
